column1: # What format-verify.sh accepts, and why. Everything else it reports is a bug.
# One line per rule, tab-separated:
#   scope   before   pattern   reason   witness
# scope    a RuboCop cop (Layout/HashAlignment) or `Comments` for a comment the
#          placement check reports as displaced.
# before   how many source lines above the offense's own line are searched
#          too, for a construct that begins earlier than the line RuboCop names.
# pattern  a Ruby regexp matched against those lines joined by newlines, or
#          `@heredoc` for an offense inside a heredoc body.
# reason   why tuxedo is right and RuboCop is not asked to agree.
# witness  the corpus project where the rule matches something. A rule applies
#          to every project, but is only checked for staleness on its witness:
#          a project that never hits it says nothing about whether it is dead.
# Layout/LineLength is not listed here: scripts/classify-linelength.rb splits
# it into the lines nothing can shorten and the ones tuxedo fails to break,
# and only the second count is a bug.
# A rule that matches nothing on its witness is reported as stale: an
# exemption that outlives what it exempted would hide the regression it was
# written to allow.
# --- A keyword used as a value ---
# `x || if c ... end`, `(class << x ... end)`, `meta = class << x`,
# `defined?(while x ... end)`: RuboCop has no style that puts `else`/`end` at
# the statement's indent, and tuxedo keeps them there (see
# format-verify.rubocop.yml). Covers the alignment and indentation cops that
# follow from it. (`when` and `begin`/`end` have the same disagreement and no
# instance on rails; add one when a project has it.)
Layout/IndentationWidth
column4: a keyword used as a value keeps its body and `end` at the statement's indent, not under the keyword

column1: Layout/EndAlignment
column4: a keyword used as a value keeps its `end` at the statement's indent

column1: Layout/ElseAlignment
column4: a keyword used as a value keeps `else`/`elsif` at the statement's indent

column1: # `method_name = def some_method\nend`: same disagreement, `def`'s own
# alignment cop.
# --- Text that is not the formatter's ---
# `# encoding: big5`, `# -*- encoding: iso-8859-9 -*-`: the file itself isn't
# valid UTF-8, so tuxedo refuses it and copies it through untouched --
# nothing it could insert a blank line into without deciding an encoding
# that isn't its call to make.
Layout/EmptyLineAfterMagicComment
column4: a magic comment naming a non-UTF-8 encoding means the file itself isn't UTF-8, and tuxedo refuses to touch a file it can't safely read

column1: Layout/SpaceInsidePercentLiteralDelimiters
column4: the content of `%x( )` is a shell command, copied verbatim

column1: Layout/ExtraSpacing
column4: the body of a heredoc is data, not code

column1: Layout/EmptyComment
column4: a bare `#` is the author's comment, and deleting one is not a formatter's job

column1: # --- Layouts that follow from block indentation ---
Layout/HashAlignment
column4: the keys of a braceless hash after `yield` continue at a fixed indent from the statement, not under the first key

column1: Layout/FirstArgumentIndentation
column4: an argument of a call on a multi-line regex literal indents from the line the call opens on, and RuboCop reads the literal's closing line as the previous one

column1: Layout/MultilineOperationIndentation
column4: the body of a block inside a condition indents from its statement, and RuboCop reads it as part of the condition

column1: # A modifier `while`/`until` whose condition wraps at an operator (the
# condition itself, not a block, is what's too long): the continuation gets
# the statement's normal single indent step, the fixed-indent rule this
# project applies everywhere, not RuboCop's doubled indent for a continued
# expression.
Layout/MultilineOperationIndentation
column4: a wrapped modifier condition indents by the statement's normal step, the same fixed indent every other break uses

column1: # `do |; c|`, `{ |; c| c }`: a block-local variable list gets the same space
# after `;` that every other list separator gets (`, `, `; ` between
# statements). RuboCop's no-space-inside-pipes style reads the semicolon as
# part of the parameter list it doesn't want touched.
Layout/SpaceAroundBlockParameters
column4: a block-local variable list is spaced like every other separator, not held to the no-space-inside-pipes style

column1:
# `if cond
  break
else
  break
end`: every branch is a jump statement, so
# nothing here falls through either way, but it is still a real two-way
# branch (property 1 forbids treating one arm as more "guarded" than the
# other) -- Tuxedo's guard clause is the narrower, single-branch case.
Layout/EmptyLineAfterGuardClause
column4: an if/else where every branch is a jump is still a branch, not the single-arm guard clause Tuxedo adds a blank line after

column1: # `module_eval { module_function }`: the access modifier is the sole
# statement of a one-line block, which has no line of its own to put a
# blank line before or after.
Layout/EmptyLinesAroundAccessModifier
column4: a bare access modifier that is the whole body of a single-line block has no line to put a blank line around

column1: # `%w(a b\` + a literal newline + `c d)`: the word list's own backslash
# continuation puts real source lines between the array's opening `%w(` and
# the code that follows it on the statement's last line. RuboCop's line
# math for these three cops reads that as the following bracketed array
# being multi-line; the array itself (`["a", "b\nc", "d"]`) is written on
# one line, and splitting the %w list would change the string it produces.
Layout/FirstArrayElementLineBreak
column4: a percent-literal's own backslash continuation, not the array after it, is what RuboCop's line count sees

column1: Layout/MultilineArrayLineBreaks
column4: a percent-literal's own backslash continuation, not the array after it, is what RuboCop's line count sees

column1: Layout/MultilineArrayBraceLayout
column4: a percent-literal's own backslash continuation, not the array after it, is what RuboCop's line count sees

column1: # `old_value, ENV["K"] = ENV["K"], "very long string"`, `git_args =
# Utils::Git.git, "-C", ...`: a value written `x = a, b, c` has no bracket
# of its own to expand into, so when it does not fit tuxedo gives it the
# same shape a bare command argument list already gets (`bare_args_doc`)
# -- the first value continues the line the assignment began on, every
# later one gets its own line. RuboCop reads the bare RHS as an array and
# wants a line break before the first element too; tuxedo keeps it
# attached on purpose, the way renaming or dropping the last value never
# reflows the first.
Layout/FirstArrayElementLineBreak
column4: a bare assignment RHS's first value stays on the line the assignment began on, like a bare command argument list's does
